_meta.note: Every fact has a source and a kind: measured (a NASA instrument), published (NASA documentation), derived (computed by us from NASA numbers). Worth checking before quoting.

facts.title: Radiation on Mars
facts.text: Curiosity's RAD instrument measured about 0.6-0.7 mSv per day on the Martian surface. Your Mars outpost uses 0.027 mSv per hour, which is the same thing: 0.65 mSv per day.

facts.title: Radiation on the way to Mars
facts.text: During the 8-month trip to Mars, RAD measured about 1.8 mSv per day. That is roughly 3 times what you get standing on the surface, because the spacecraft is not shielded by a planet or atmosphere.
facts.source: NASA MSL/RAD cruise data (Zeitlin et al., Science 2013)

facts.title: Radiation on the Moon
facts.text: A lander on the far side of the Moon measured about 1.37 mSv per day. That is 2 times the Mars surface. The Moon has no air to stop particles. Your Moon outpost uses 0.057 mSv per hour. (This instrument flew on China's Chang'e-4, with German scientists; NASA's LRO satellite also measures lunar radiation.)
facts.source: Chang'e-4 LND (Zhang et al., Science Advances 2020); NASA LRO CRaTER

facts.title: Radiation on the space station
facts.text: Astronauts on the International Space Station receive about 80 mSv during a six-month stay. A dental X-ray is about 0.005 mSv.
facts.source: NASA Space Radiation / Human Research Program

facts.title: Why there is a dose limit
facts.text: NASA's career limit for astronauts is 600 mSv. Your game limit is 250 mSv, scaled down so that one big storm during a short 72-96 hour mission really matters.

facts.title: Flare classes: C, M and X
facts.text: Solar flares are ranked C (small), M (medium) and X (biggest). Each letter is 10 times stronger than the one before. In this game C is a minor storm, M is moderate and X is severe.

facts.title: Why warnings give you time
facts.text: Light from a flare reaches us in about 8 minutes, but the dangerous particles can take from minutes to hours to arrive. Forecasters at NASA and NOAA use that gap to warn astronauts to shelter.
facts.source: NASA Space Weather Research Center / DONKI

facts.title: Talking to Earth takes time
facts.text: A radio message to Mars takes between about 3 and 22 minutes one way, depending on where the planets are. To the Moon it takes about 1.3 seconds. So a Mars crew cannot ask Mission Control for help in real time: they have to decide themselves.
facts.source: Computed from JPL approximate planetary positions

facts.title: What is a sol?
facts.text: A sol is one Mars day: 24 hours 39 minutes 35 seconds. NASA mission teams on Mars live by sols, so their schedule slides about 40 minutes every day.

facts.title: Sunshine on Mars
facts.text: Mars is farther from the Sun, so its sunlight is only about 43% as strong as at Earth (about 590 vs 1361 watts per square metre at the top of the sky). Dust makes it dimmer still, so the solar panels have to be big.

facts.title: Dust on solar panels
facts.text: Dust slowly covers solar panels on Mars. NASA's Spirit and Opportunity rovers sometimes got lucky when a gust of wind cleaned them. A human crew would have to sweep them: that is the Clean panels button.

facts.title: The storm that stopped Opportunity
facts.text: In 2018 a giant dust storm blocked so much sunlight that the Opportunity rover's batteries ran dry and it stopped talking to Earth. Power is life on Mars.

facts.title: The Twins Study
facts.text: NASA compared astronaut Scott Kelly, who spent almost a year on the space station, with his identical twin Mark on Earth. They found changes in gene activity, the gut and the immune system, and most went back to normal after the return.
facts.source: NASA Twins Study (Garrett-Bakelman et al., Science 2019); data in NASA OSDR

facts.title: NASA's open lab notebook
facts.text: The Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) shares data from spaceflight biology experiments on plants, mice, microbes and human cells. Anyone can search it, including you.

facts.title: Growing food in space
facts.text: In 2015 astronauts on the space station ate red romaine lettuce that they had grown themselves in the Veggie plant chamber. Fresh food also helps morale on long missions.

facts.title: Bones in space
facts.text: In microgravity astronauts can lose about 1 to 1.5 percent of bone density in the hips and spine every month, so they exercise about 2 hours a day.

facts.title: Moon dirt as a shield
facts.text: NASA studies piling regolith (Moon or Mars soil) over habitats to block radiation. That is the berm: it costs work and time, and it protects the crew all day and all night.
